item.title: Awa Jurobe Yashiki: Traditional Puppet Theatre — Guide
item.description: Tokushima, old Awa, has one of Japan’s richest traditions of ningyo joruri — the art of puppet theatre, in which large, elaborately costumed puppets are brought to life by teams of skilled puppeteers, accompanied by chanted narration and shamisen music. Once hugely popular in the region’s villages, with rural stages at many shrines, the art survives here as a living tradition. Awa Jurobe Yashiki, on the site of a historic residence in Tokushima city, is the place to experience it: daily performances stage the region’s most famous puppet play, and you can see the intricate puppets up close, watch the puppeteers at work, and learn about the craft.

item.title: Hagi Museums: History, Art and the Meiji Story — Guide
item.description: For a town of its size, Hagi has an outstanding array of museums that together tell its remarkable story. The Hagi Museum, in the old castle district, covers the town’s history, natural heritage and its extraordinary role in the Meiji Restoration, the revolution that toppled the shogunate and built modern Japan — several of whose leaders were Hagi men. Nearby, the Hagi Uragami Museum is a distinguished art museum known for its collection of ukiyo-e woodblock prints and Asian ceramics.

item.title: Kimono Rental in Asakusa — Guide
item.description: Renting a kimono in Asakusa is one of Tokyo’s most popular and enjoyable cultural experiences, letting you explore the atmospheric old-town streets around Senso-ji Temple dressed in beautiful traditional attire. Numerous rental shops cluster around Asakusa, offering a huge range of kimono (and yukata in summer) for men, women and children, with plans that typically include help getting dressed by staff, coordinated obi sashes and accessories, and often hair styling for an extra fee.

item.title: Kumamoto Art Museums near the Castle — Guide
item.description: In the castle district of central Kumamoto, close to the great fortress, art museums offer a refined cultural experience amid the city’s historic heart. Set near the Ōtemon (main gate) area and castle grounds, these galleries present a mix of modern and contemporary Japanese and Western art, works by artists connected to Kumamoto and the wider region, and changing special exhibitions, in calm, well-designed spaces. They provide an elegant contrast to the castle’s martial history and the greenery of its grounds, and are an ideal addition for visitors who enjoy art and want a quieter, indoor cultural stop between the castle, gardens and city sights.

item.title: Nagasaki Museum of History and Culture — Guide
item.description: The Nagasaki Museum of History and Culture, in the Tateyama district, is devoted to the city’s remarkable history as Japan’s principal gateway for overseas trade and cultural exchange during its centuries of isolation. Its well-designed exhibits explore how goods, people, religions and ideas from China, the Netherlands and beyond flowed through Nagasaki, shaping a uniquely cosmopolitan local culture — from imported art and crafts to the fusion food and festivals still seen today.

item.title: Okinawa World & Gyokusendo Cave — Guide
item.description: Okinawa World, in Nanjo in southern Okinawa, is a large cultural theme park that showcases the nature, crafts and traditions of the Ryukyu Islands, built around one of Japan’s most impressive limestone caves. Its centrepiece is Gyokusendo Cave, an enormous, ancient cavern where a roughly 890-metre walkway winds past a dazzling forest of stalactites, stalagmites and underground pools, dramatically illuminated — one of the largest and most beautiful show caves in the country.

item.title: Ryukyu Dance Performance — Guide
item.description: Ryukyu dance (Ryukyu buyo) is the elegant traditional performing art of the Ryukyu Kingdom, developed over centuries and refined at the royal court, where it was once performed to entertain envoys from China and Japan. Graceful, stately and expressive, it is danced in gorgeous, richly coloured costumes — often including bingata-dyed kimono and distinctive headwear — to the haunting music of the sanshin (a snakeskin-covered three-stringed lute), drums and song. The repertoire ranges from refined, slow-moving classical court dances to livelier, more rhythmic folk dances (zo-odori) full of energy and charm, sometimes with props like fans, hats or bamboo clappers.

item.title: Tea Ceremony Experience — Guide
item.description: A Japanese tea ceremony (chado or sado, ‘the way of tea’) is a refined, meditative ritual centred on the preparation and serving of matcha (powdered green tea), and taking part in one is a wonderful way to experience the depth and mindfulness of Japanese culture. Across Tokyo, tea houses, cultural centres and specialist studios offer tea ceremony experiences designed for visitors, many with English-speaking hosts. In a tranquil tatami room, a kimono-clad host demonstrates the graceful, precise movements of preparing the tea, explaining the etiquette, philosophy and seasonal aesthetics behind each gesture — the emphasis on harmony, respect, purity and tranquillity.

item.title: The Shikoku 88-Temple Pilgrimage in Kochi — Guide
item.description: The Shikoku Pilgrimage is Japan’s most famous walking pilgrimage, a 1,200-kilometre circuit of 88 temples associated with the revered monk Kobo Daishi (Kukai), who was born on the island. Each of Shikoku’s four prefectures represents a stage of spiritual progress, and Kochi — old Tosa — is the longest and most demanding, known as the ‘dojo of ascetic training’. Its 16 temples are spread far apart along a wild stretch of Pacific coast and mountains, from Cape Muroto in the east to Cape Ashizuri in the far south, testing the pilgrim’s endurance and resolve.

item.title: Tottori Folklore Museum: The Region's Folk Craft — Guide
item.description: Tottori has an unusually strong folk-craft identity, thanks in large part to Yoshida Shoya, a local doctor and disciple of the Mingei (folk craft) movement who championed the beauty of everyday, handmade objects across the region in the twentieth century. The prefecture’s folklore and folk-craft museums preserve and display this heritage: the everyday tools, textiles, ceramics, woodwork and household objects of ordinary Tottori life, chosen for the honest beauty of things made by hand for use.

item.title: Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art — Guide
item.description: The Tottori Prefectural Museum of Art is the prefecture’s flagship art museum, a strikingly modern building in Kurayoshi in central Tottori that has quickly become a cultural anchor for the region. Its collection and changing exhibitions span the art of Tottori and the wider San’in region alongside modern and contemporary Japanese and international works, and its architecture — light-filled, open and designed as a public gathering space as much as a gallery — is part of the appeal.

item.title: Ueno Park — Guide
item.description: Ueno Park (Ueno Onshi Koen) is one of Tokyo’s largest and most important public parks, a spacious green expanse that doubles as the city’s premier cluster of museums and cultural institutions. Within its grounds are the Tokyo National Museum (Japan’s oldest and largest), the National Museum of Western Art, the National Museum of Nature and Science, and several art museums, along with Ueno Zoo, historic shrines and temples, and Shinobazu Pond with its summer lotuses and boats.

item.title: Yamaguchi City Culture and Arts Center — Guide
item.description: Yamaguchi city, the prefectural capital, has long prided itself on culture, once nicknamed the ‘Kyoto of the West’ for its refinement in the medieval era. Today that spirit continues in its modern cultural and arts facilities, which host changing exhibitions, concerts and performances, and programmes of international exchange, all in a contemporary setting in the heart of the city. For travellers, a stop here offers a glimpse of the region’s living cultural scene beyond its historic temples and gardens — a chance to catch an exhibition or event, learn about local arts, and see how a quiet provincial capital keeps its long cultural tradition alive in the present day.

item.title: Yufuin Art Museums & Galleries — Guide
item.description: Part of what gives Yufuin its distinctive artsy, upscale character is the cluster of small art museums and galleries scattered through the town, which set it apart from other hot-spring resorts. Along and just off the main street, visitors can discover an eclectic mix: elegant fine-art museums displaying Japanese and Western paintings, ceramics and sculpture, sometimes in beautiful garden settings; small private galleries and craft studios; and a range of quirky, fun themed museums that Yufuin is also known for.

item.title: Kyoto Kimono Rental Guide: Dressing the Part in the Old Capital
item.description: There is no more atmospheric way to explore Kyoto’s historic streets than dressed in a kimono. As you walk the stone lanes of Higashiyama or cross a bridge in Arashiyama, the traditional silhouette transforms the experience — and the photographs. Kimono rental in Kyoto is easy, affordable, and hugely popular with visitors of every nationality and gender: shops dress you head to toe, style your hair, and send you out for the day.

item.title: Kyoto Kodo Guide: The Incense Ceremony, Japan's Subtlest Art
item.description: Alongside the tea ceremony and flower arranging, Japan has a third classical art that few visitors ever discover: kodo (the “way of incense”). In kodo, participants don’t “smell” incense — they “listen” to it, savouring the faint, evolving fragrance of precious heated woods like agarwood with full, meditative attention. Refined among Kyoto’s aristocracy over centuries, kodo is the most subtle and rarefied of the traditional arts, and the city’s historic incense houses offer visitors a rare chance to experience it.

item.title: Kyoto Maiko Makeover Guide: Transform Into a Geiko for a Day
item.description: In Kyoto you can be transformed into a maiko — an apprentice geiko (Kyoto’s word for geisha) — for an afternoon of beautiful photographs. The maiko makeover (henshin, “transformation”) experience is a popular studio activity in which professional artists apply the iconic white makeup, dress you in an elaborate maiko kimono and obi, fit a traditional wig and ornaments, and photograph you in studio or out on Kyoto’s historic streets. It’s a memorable, only-in-Kyoto way to step into one of Japan’s most enduring images of elegance.

item.title: Kyoto Tea Ceremony Guide: Experiencing Chado as a Visitor
item.description: The Japanese tea ceremony (chado, “the way of tea,” also chanoyu) is far more than drinking matcha — it is a centuries-old art of hospitality, mindfulness, and aesthetics in which every gesture, object, and seasonal detail is considered. Kyoto is its heartland: the city is home to the great tea schools that have shaped the practice for centuries, and there is no better place to experience it. For visitors, a tea ceremony offers a quiet, profound window into the Japanese sense of beauty — and many studios now offer warm, beginner-friendly sessions in English.

item.title: Osaka Kendo Class Guide: Try the Way of the Sword
item.description: Behind the thunderous shouts and clashing bamboo of a dojo lies kendo — “the way of the sword,” the modern martial art descended from samurai swordsmanship. A kendo experience class in Osaka lets visitors step onto the dojo floor, grip the bamboo shinai, learn a few basic cuts and stances, and even try on a piece of the armour, all under an instructor who explains the discipline, spirit, and etiquette behind it.

item.title: Sanshin Guide: Okinawa's Banjo, Lessons & Where to Hear It
item.description: The sanshin is the soul of Okinawan music — a three-stringed, snakeskin-covered “banjo” whose warm, twanging sound underpins everything from gentle folk ballads to the driving beat of eisa. An ancestor of the mainland shamisen, it has been central to Ryukyu culture for centuries. For visitors, a beginner sanshin lesson is a delightful, hands-on way to connect with the island’s spirit — you’ll learn to hold it, read the kunkunshi notation, and pluck out a simple Okinawan tune in under an hour.

item.title: Okinawa Festivals Guide: Eisa, Dragon Boats, Lanterns & Ryukyuan Ceremonies
item.description: Okinawa’s festival calendar reflects its unique heritage — Ryukyuan religious ceremonies, Obon customs distinct from mainland Japan, and a performance tradition centred on the eisa drum dance and sanshin music that has no equivalent anywhere else. The events are not recreations for tourists; they are living community traditions. 旧盆エイサー — Okinawan Eisa (Obon Period) When: Three days of Obon by the lunar calendar — typically mid-to-late August Where: Every village and neighbourhood across Okinawa; biggest in Okinawa City (Koza)

item.title: Okinawa Sightseeing Guide: Shuri Castle, Ryukyu Heritage & Hidden Spots
item.description: Okinawa’s history is unlike anywhere else in Japan. For 450 years (1429–1879) it was the independent Ryukyu Kingdom — a maritime trading nation with its own language, religion, architecture, and performing arts. The Ryukyuan legacy is everywhere: in the bright red lacquer of its castles (gusuku), the sound of the sanshin (three-stringed lute), and a cuisine built on tropical ingredients rather than the rice and soy of mainland Japan. 1.
